prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, enabling atomic timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a distinct invention: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the conflict between tight Lamb-Dicke confinement and light shifts, and Ye's group turned it into the most accurate and stable measuring instrument built so far, at roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. It is a discovery-and-invention package with unusually clean two-person credit, confirmed by many independent laboratories and by clock-to-clock comparisons, and it has reach beyond atomic physics into tests of fundamental constants and variation, relativistic geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second. It is also the one candidate on the shortlist where the credit question is not a serious problem: the supplied names are the two people most colleagues would name. As someone who has spent a career on coherent light-matter interaction and on the limits of what can be measured, I judge it the strongest case on the list, while recognising that this is my own field and I should discount my enthusiasm accordingly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier recognition. Hall and Hansch (2005, combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control) cover much of the enabling toolkit, and a committee could read lattice clocks as a refinement of recognised precision-spectroscopy physics rather than a new principle. There is also a timing argument that the redefinition of the second has not happened, and ion-clock groups and other early lattice-clock contributors sit outside the credited names. Finally, B047 has the narrowest opening support after B006: only four of eight members ranked it, and it is outside the interest of the condensed-matter members, so I should not read my own first place as consensus.

responses.point: Ranked B034 second and B006 first; argues that ultracold-atom lattices are a statistical-physics laboratory with lasting impact, and that overlap with trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates may favour a single combined quantum-simulation award.
responses.response: I ranked B034 fifth, so I agree on the quality of the physics but not on its priority. The superfluid-Mott transition and the microscope are real, but the decisive scientific payoff, solving problems beyond classical reach, has not yet arrived, and Bloch/Greiner/Zoller would also overlap in Zoller with B031 as I noted in my own ballot. The credit for the Mott proposal (Jaksch and others) is also spread beyond three. Combining quantum simulation with ion-based computing would give a diffuse citation. I think a sharply defined invention with a quantified result, as in B047, is the safer prize.

responses.point: Ranked B047 third and flags overlap with earlier prizes for frequency combs and ion clocks, and whether the clock is a distinct invention or an incremental refinement.
responses.response: This is the fair objection and I take it seriously. My answer is that combs (2005) are the readout gearwork and the Al+ ion clock is a different system with a different confinement problem; the lattice clock solves the problem of using many neutral atoms simultaneously with no first-order light shift, which is what gave the order-of-magnitude gain in stability through averaging. Magic-wavelength trapping is a new principle, not tuning. I accept that the citation must be worded around that invention rather than around 'better clocks', and I have drafted it that way. I would value her view on whether the ion-clock community's claim ought to change the credited names.

responses.point: Ranked B047 first with me; stresses the redefinition of the second and asks whether the committee would prefer to wait for it, and competing ion-clock claims.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the two names. On waiting, I disagree mildly: the Nobel criterion is the discovery and its demonstrated impact, not a metrology-body decision, and clock comparisons already confirm the claim. Waiting for the redefinition risks the prize following the metrologists instead of leading them. I do accept her point that the ion-clock community is a legitimate adjacent claim, and as two atomic physicists on this committee we should make sure neither of us is judged to be reviewing our own neighbourhood without outside challenge.

responses.point: Ranked B038 first, arguing circuit QED is a clean idea with large downstream impact and is distinct from the 2025 prize, though some spacing may be wise.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is a clean transfer of cavity QED and that the Blais/Wallraff/Schoelkopf trio is sound; I ranked it third. My reservation is that it is an enabling architecture whose scientific discoveries are partly the prize-recognised 2025 circuit work, and Girvin's omission and the Devoret lineage make the credit less clean than for B047. If the committee wants a quantum-technology prize this year, I would accept B038 or B031 over a condensed-matter choice, but I do not think it displaces the measurement case.

responses.point: Ranked B017 first as a clean prediction-plus-experiment prize, noting open questions on superconducting pairing and other groups' roles.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is an elegant story and I ranked it seventh mainly on maturity: the pairing mechanism is unresolved and the experimental credit is complicated by Cao and Dean's work not being on the list. I do not see a defect in the concept, only that it is early; if the committee waits five to ten years, the claim will be stronger rather than weaker.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the earlier recognised comb and ion-control metrology prizes.
Precedence among early lattice-clock proposals and demonstrations is from memory and was not independently verified; whether additional names beyond Katori and Ye would be argued.
Four of eight members did not rank B047; it is unclear whether condensed-matter members would regard it as comparable in breadth to B006.
statement.conflict_note: Possible connections to flag: my doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is closely tied to the precision-spectroscopy and frequency-comb lineage that Jun Ye's work belongs to, so I may have a scientific-lineage affinity for B047, though no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye is documented in my profile. Separately, my Lund quantum-information work, European quantum-memory collaborations and WACQT role relate to the B031 and B038 alternatives, which may call for recusal discussion if those are chosen.
